title: hardware-bench-cloud-sku-driver-matrix
content:
Purpose and high-level summary:

This is a working note capturing the hardware-comparison benchmark matrix we ran across A100 / H100 / L40S class GPUs on multiple cloud SKUs and with a few driver+CUDA permutations. Goal was to reproduce realistic inference workloads (small-batch streaming and batched throughput) and surface systematic differences that affect Redwood’s serving runtime choices (kernel selection, batching policy defaults, and fallback routing).

Key takeaways (short):
- H100 shows consistently lower tail latency for long context runs (>=2048) when using CUDA 12.x + driver 535+ on p5-like hardware, but throughput advantage vs A100 depends heavily on NVLink topology and multi-GPU batching strategy.
- A100 (p4d / GCP A2-style) tends to be more cost-effective for sustained throughput with our fp16/4-bit quantized paths; its kernel maturity gives predictable latency for short requests.
- L40S (GCP L-series / some cloud L40 SKUs) is surprisingly strong for mixed workloads (embed + generate concurrently) due to higher VRAM and good fp16 kernel coverage; however driver/CUDA mismatches caused a few outlier stalls in our early runs.
- Driver/CUDA combinations matter: we observed a 6-12% difference in token/sec between CUDA 11.8 + driver 520.x vs CUDA 12.2 + driver 535.x on identical A100 SKUs for our MLP-heavy attention kernels.

Environment and reproducibility notes:
- Model baseline used: LLM families emulating 7B/13B/70B inference shapes. For each model size we ran:
  * short: seq_len=64, batch=1..8 (interactive streaming)
  * medium: seq_len=512, batch=1..4
  * long: seq_len=2048, batch=1..2 (LLR tasks)
- Runtimes: Redwood serving runtime HEAD (commit rwd/serving@main:9b3d), PyTorch 2.2 (for CPU orchestration), triton inference libraries where applicable.
- Profiling tools: nsys (Nsight Systems), ncu (Nsight Compute) for kernel-level metrics, and per-request tracing via our runtime trace hooks. Collected: kernel time, SM occupancy, tensor-core utilization, cudaMemcpy durations, PCIe stall times, and CPU->GPU copy latencies.
- Example profiling command used (nsys):
  nsys profile --trace=cuda,osrt --output profile-A100-p4d --sample=none --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi -- python run_bench.py --model Llama-13B --seq 2048 --batch 1

Cloud SKUs tested (representative):
- AWS: p4d.24xlarge (A100), p5.24xlarge (H100)
- GCP: a2-highgpu-1g / a2-highgpu-8g (A100), l4 (L40S-like types)
- Azure: ND A100 v4-style nodes, NCasv5/H100 variants where available

Driver+CUDA matrix (selected combos):
- CUDA 11.8 + NVIDIA driver 520.x (baseline A100 stable stack)
- CUDA 11.8 + driver 525.x (compatibility check)
- CUDA 12.2 + driver 535.x (H100-optimized stack)
- CUDA 12.3 + driver 540.x (experimental on L40S testbeds)

Microbench design and measurements (representative numbers — median over 3 runs):
- Model: Llama-like 13B, quantized fp16 path (no KV-cache compression)
  * A100 (p4d), CUDA11.8/520: short seq batch=1 => p99 latency 45ms, throughput ~18 tokens/sec (streaming). medium seq batch=2 => ~320 tokens/sec.
  * H100 (p5), CUDA12.2/535: short seq batch=1 => p99 latency 38ms, throughput ~22 tokens/sec. long seq batch=1 => p99 latency improvement ~9-12% vs A100.
  * L40S (GCP l4), CUDA12.3/540: short seq batch=1 => p99 latency 50ms (higher startup), but throughput scales better for mixed workloads, sustained token/sec similar to A100 for medium sequence.
- Model: 70B-class (memory-bound) using sharded single-GPU configs to stress memory bandwidth
  * A100 shows expected out-of-core paging earlier; H100's HBM bandwidth advantage reduced some KV cache misses but only when kernels reused tensor-core-optimized GEMMs.

Observed bottlenecks and kernel-level notes:
- PCIe host<->GPU copy dominates latency for small-batch streaming when CPU tensor prep isn't overlapped correctly. Many cloud SKUs with older CPUs / PCIe gen3 hurt short-request p99.
- NVLink/NVSwitch topologies beneficial for multi-GPU batched throughput; our batching strategy must be topology-aware to avoid cross-switch hops.
- Driver+CUDA mismatches created kernel selector fallbacks in CuBLAS/CuDNN: we saw runtime fallback to non-tensor-core kernels on a patched driver on one H100 image, increasing token/sec variance.
- Kernel launch overheads (many small kernels due to autograd-free inference pipelines) significantly affect short-seq latency; kernel fusion (where safe) reduces overhead by ~20% in our microbench.

Anomalies encountered (investigation notes):
- On one L40S image with driver 540.x we saw sporadic spikes (~300-400ms) attributable to device-side memory compaction triggered by driver GC — reproduced with nsys showing long cudaMemFree stalls. Hypothesis: driver bug interacting with our allocator and pinned memory. Action: reproduce with NVIDIA support and try different allocator knobs (cudaHostAlloc flags / UVM off).
- On older A100 images (customer-provided AMIs) tensor-core kernels compiled against mixed-libs caused 10% worse throughput vs canonical vendor image; remediation: enforce a minimal vendor image baseline or containerize with vendor-provided CUDA runtime.

Experiment matrix (what we ran, condensed):
- For each SKU x driver x CUDA x model-size x seq-length x batch-size we collected: p50/p90/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU util, avg SM occupancy, memcpy breakdown, kernel-wise time slices.
- Total runs: ~720 end-to-end runs across all combos (each run ~10-15 minutes).

Practical recommendations for the serving runtime (based on these runs):
1) Maintain a mapping of SKU -> recommended driver+CUDA in our model catalog. For example: p5/H100 -> CUDA12.2 + driver 535.x, p4d/A100 -> CUDA11.8 + driver 520.x, GCP L40S -> CUDA12.3 + driver 540.x (experimental).
2) Add topology-aware batching: detect NVLink/NVSwitch and prefer intra-node multi-GPU batches to reduce cross-switch latency.
3) Add short-request fast-path: avoid host-side copies and fuse small kernels; prioritize kernel fusion for seq<=128 + batch<=4.
4) Harden our container images: pin CUDA runtime and CuBLAS versions used in the benchmark; provide validated images per SKU to customers (or in Dedicated).
5) Feature-flag driver-level fallback tracing in the console to surface kernel fallback events (non-tensor-core kernels) as a quality/regression signal.

Next steps / follow-ups:
- Re-run subset with our allocator changes (pinned-memory policy) to see if L40S cudaMemFree stalls disappear.
- Build an automated daily smoke on representative SKUs to detect regressions from driver updates (CI job that runs short/medium tests and validates token/sec tolerance).
- File NVIDIA support tickets for the L40S driver behavior and attach nsys captures.

Notes to reviewers / open questions:
- How aggressive do we want to be on recommending newer CUDA for Dedicated customers vs sticking to the oldest common denom for stability? (tradeoff: improved H100 perf vs increased risk of regressions)
- For pricing models: should we automatically route long-job low-concurrency runs to H100 SKUs if a customer has multi-SKU access? (requires routing policy + cost calc).

Raw attachments (stored separately): full nsys traces, per-kernel CSV exports, and the run scripts are in GH PR linked above. If you want a quick reproduce: run run_bench.py with --profile and the SKU env to replay.

Sign-off:
Ethan Chen (eng-serving-runtime) — draft notes, please add counter-experiments.
